name: No Timing
explanation: This is the strictest version of the timing criteria. Timing can't be a required part of completing the activity at all, not even with a way to extend it. There are two narrow exceptions. One is non-interactive synchronized media, like a pre-recorded video with captions, where timing is fundamental to the content itself. The other is genuine real-time events, like a live auction, where a delay would defeat the purpose. Outside those two exceptions, if a user could still finish the task given unlimited time, then no time limit should exist at all.
whoItAffects: Some people process information more slowly than others. This can be due to a cognitive disability, a motor disability, unfamiliarity with the interface, or assistive technology that takes more steps to complete an action. All of these people benefit from never facing a countdown at all. This goes further than SC 2.2.1's adjustable-timing accommodation. Rather than requiring the user to notice a warning and act on it in time, this removes the pressure entirely. That matters most for tasks like completing a purchase, filling out a long form, or taking an assessment.
howToTest: Find any task on the site with a time limit of any kind. This includes ones that already meet SC 2.2.1 by offering extensions or warnings. For each one, ask whether the underlying activity is a genuine real-time event, like bidding in a live auction, or non-interactive synchronized media, like watching a captioned video. If it's neither of those, this AAA criterion requires removing the time limit altogether, not just making it adjustable.

check.question: A job application form gives users 15 minutes to complete it, with a warning and the ability to request a 15-minute extension before time runs out — satisfying SC 2.2.1. Does this also satisfy the stricter SC 2.2.3 No Timing?
choices: Yes, because meeting SC 2.2.1 automatically satisfies SC 2.2.3
No, because SC 2.2.3 requires no time limit at all for a non-real-time, non-synchronized-media activity like this
Yes, because 15 minutes plus an extension is generous enough
It depends only on whether the extension can be requested more than once
